title: The Skull
question: Which bone is glowing?
lines: Can you name the glowing skull bone?
Look at the side of the skull.
Which bone is it?
It sits at the side of the head, around the ear.
Your jaw hinges on it, just in front of your ear.
It's D. The temporal bone.
Why it matters: it protects your inner ear, for hearing and balance.

title: The Skull
question: Which bone is glowing?
lines: Only one skull bone really moves. Can you name it?
It's the bone that's glowing.
Which bone is it?
The maxilla holds your upper teeth, and it doesn't move.
This bone holds the lower teeth and hinges to open your mouth.
It's B. The mandible.
Why it matters: it's the largest, strongest bone in your face.

title: The Skull
question: Which bone is glowing?
lines: You can feel this bone right now. Name it.
Watch the small bone that's glowing.
Which bone is it?
It's not the maxilla, which holds your upper teeth.
This one forms the bump of your cheek.
It's C. The zygomatic bone, your cheekbone.
Why it matters: it shapes your face and guards your eye socket.

title: The Skull
question: Which bone is glowing?
lines: The back of your skull has its own bone. Do you know it?
Watch the glowing bone at the back of the head.
Which bone is glowing?
The parietal bones sit on top. This one is lower.
It also has the big opening where the spinal cord passes through.
It's B. The occipital bone.
Why it matters: it protects the part of the brain that handles vision.

title: The Skull
question: Which bones are glowing?
lines: Put your hand on top of your head. You're touching these bones.
Look at the glowing pair across the top of the head.
Which bones are glowing?
The temporal bones sit lower, around the ears.
It's C. The parietal bones.
Why it matters: they protect the top of the brain and meet at the midline.

title: The Skull
question: Which bone holds the upper teeth?
lines: Smile. Your top teeth are anchored in this bone.
Look at the glowing pair of bones around the upper jaw.
Which bone holds the upper teeth?
The lower teeth sit in the mandible, the only moving skull bone.
It's B. The maxilla, a pair joined at the midline.
Why it matters: they also form most of the roof of your mouth.

title: The Skull
question: Which bone is glowing?
lines: Touch your forehead. You can feel this bone right now.
Watch the glowing bone at the front of the skull.
Which bone is glowing?
The parietal bones sit behind it, on top of the head.
It's A. The frontal bone, which forms the forehead.
Why it matters: it protects the front of the brain and the eyes.

title: The Skull
question: How many bones form the face?
lines: Your face is built from a lot of small bones. How many?
Watch the glowing bones of the face and jaw.
How many bones form the face?
Eight is the number of bones around the brain.
Count the jaw, cheeks, nose, eye sockets and palate together.
It's C. Fourteen facial bones.
Why it matters: they shape your face and hold your teeth.

title: The Skull
question: Which bone is shaped like a butterfly?
lines: One skull bone is shaped like a butterfly. Can you find it?
It sits at the base of the skull, reaching out toward the temples.
Which bone is shaped like a butterfly?
The ethmoid is a small, spongy bone between the eyes.
Its wings spread to both sides of the skull and touch many other bones.
It's B. The sphenoid bone.
Why it matters: it links many skull bones together like a keystone.

title: The Skull
question: What's its everyday name?
lines: You use this bone every time you talk or chew. What's it called?
Watch the glowing bone at the bottom of the face.
What's its everyday name?
The cheekbone is higher up, under the eye.
This is the only skull bone that moves a lot when you open your mouth.
It's D. The jawbone, or mandible.
Why it matters: it lets you chew and speak.

title: The Skull
question: How many bones form the cranium?
lines: Your brain sits inside a bony case. How many bones make it?
Watch the glowing bones that wrap around the brain.
How many bones form the cranium?
The face bones are a separate group. This one wraps the brain.
Count: frontal, 2 parietal, 2 temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid.
It's A. Eight bones.
Why it matters: they form the protective case around the brain.

title: The Skull
question: Which two bones are glowing?
lines: Smile and feel the bones that make your cheeks stand out.
Watch the two bones glowing at the sides of the face.
Which two bones are they?
The maxillae sit in the middle, holding the upper teeth.
These two form the prominence of your cheeks.
It's D. The zygomatic bones.
Why it matters: they form part of the eye sockets' outer rim.

title: The Skull
question: Which bone has the hole for the spinal cord?
lines: Your brain meets your spinal cord through one hole in the skull.
Watch the glowing bone at the back and base of the skull.
Which bone has that hole?
The sphenoid sits in the middle of the skull base, further forward.
The big opening, the foramen magnum, is in this bone.
It's C. The occipital bone.
Why it matters: the spinal cord leaves the skull through this opening.

title: The Skull
question: How many skull bones, not ear bones?
lines: Your head looks like one solid piece. It isn't.
Every bone glowing here is a separate bone of the adult skull.
How many bones is that?
Thirty-three is the count for the whole spine, not the skull.
Eight in the cranium plus fourteen in the face.
It's B. Twenty-two.
Why it matters: most skull bones lock together at joints that barely move.
